title: Jeff Dean leaves Google after 27 years for Discovery Loop as DeepMind leadership reshuffles
subtitle: Alphabet moves Demis Hassabis to Chief Scientist and hands day-to-day Gemini leadership to Koray Kavukcuoglu, while Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc Le exit to launch a public-benefit startup that aims to automate scientific research.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Alphabet announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division on August 5. Demis Hassabis moves from CEO of Google DeepMind to Chair of DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet. Koray Kavukcuoglu becomes SVP of Google DeepMind and takes day-to-day operational control of the Gemini model family. On the same day, Jeff Dean — Google's chief scientist and its second employee to work on large-scale ML systems — announced he is leaving after 27 years, along with Google senior fellow Sanjay Ghemawat, DeepMind research VP Oriol Vinyals, and Google Brain co-founder Quoc Le. The four are launching Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation, with backing from Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures. Google will serve as a founding investor and cloud partner. Alphabet's stock closed down roughly 5% on the news, wiping out about $160-200 billion in market capitalization.

Discovery Loop's stated mission is to automate the scientific research loop — proposing experiments, running them, evaluating results, and iterating — first for ML research itself, then for hardware design, drug discovery, and clean energy. That framing puts the company in direct competition with efforts inside DeepMind (AlphaFold's successors, the Gemini for Science tooling) and Anthropic (which has published on automated research agents). The founding team's combined depth in distributed systems (Dean, Ghemawat wrote MapReduce and Bigtable), reinforcement learning (Vinyals led AlphaStar), and neural architecture (Le co-authored the original Transformer paper and Google Brain's early work) is unusual — most AI-agents-for-science startups are founded by domain scientists, not by the people who built the infrastructure the field runs on.

The context is a rough summer for Google DeepMind. The flagship next-generation Gemini model remained unreleased despite a planned June launch, drawing investor and reporter questions about whether Google was losing pace with Anthropic and OpenAI. Hassabis's move to Chief Scientist is being described inside the company as a return to hands-on research, but from the outside it looks like a decoupling of research and product — with Kavukcuoglu owning the shipping and Hassabis owning the science. Losing Dean and Ghemawat also thins Google's infrastructure bench in a period when compute pipelines and custom silicon are the industry's central battleground.

For learners: when a technical founder-figure at a major lab moves from operational to research-only, watch what happens in the following two quarters. Sometimes the move frees them to solve the hardest problems the org has been sitting on; sometimes it precedes an exit. And when four of your most senior researchers leave together — with a plan, a name, and outside funding already lined up — the announcement was the polite ending, not the start. If you are early in your career, the more actionable lesson is who is building Discovery Loop's founding team: Google's willingness to remain an investor and cloud provider suggests the split is amicable, and history says the first 20 hires at a lab like this go on to define an entire subfield.
